chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus, from Sama'ah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him: 'A man leaves behind for his family an allowance of three thousand dirhams, which is their sustenance for years; is Zakat due upon it?' He said: 'If he was present (at the time of Zakat due), Zakat is due upon it; and if he was absent, there is nothing upon it.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And if the Muslim does not find a believer entitled to Zakat, and it has become obligatory upon him, and he finds a believing slave being sold, he buys him with the Zakat money and frees him. And likewise, if he finds one entitled to Zakat, but he sees a believing slave in need, he buys him with his Zakat and frees him; this suffices him. This is indicated by what was narrated:'

key_terms.شَاهِد: Present (one who was present when Zakat was due)
key_terms.غَائِب: Absent (one who was away/unaware when Zakat was due)

ai.seo_question: Is Zakat due on the wealth of a deceased person who died without paying it?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the timing of Zakat liability based on the deceased's presence, a key distinction in Shia jurisprudence for estate distribution. Shaykh al-Tusi adds that Zakat can be utilized for manumission of a believing slave if no direct recipients are available, highlighting the flexibility of Zakat funds in fulfilling social obligations. This reflects the broader Shia principle that Zakat serves both charitable and emancipatory purposes when distributed by the Imam or his deputies.
